newsitem.title: USA: Rubin says strong dollar in U.S. interest.
newsitem.headline: Rubin says strong dollar in U.S. interest.

text.p: Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin said on Tuesday a strong dollar is in the United States' interest and that he was not concerned about the potential effect of a strong dollar on the U.S. trade deficit.

Rubin, speaking to a group of reporters, also said that he believed it was likely that the White House and Congress could reach agreement on a balanced budget, but added that this did not mean it was certain they would do so.
He described Clinton's fiscal 1998 budget proposal, due to be sent to Congress on Feb. 6, as "sound and sensible."
Rubin said it was in the interest of both Japan and the United States that Japan enjoy good growth, adding he believed it was important Japanese growth be led by domestic demand.

Asked to comment on Japanese Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka's remark that the weakness of the yen is overdone, Rubin replied with his long-standing comment that: "We believe a strong dollar is in our national economic self-interest."

Asked if he was concerned about the effect of a strong dollar on the U.S. trade deficit, Rubin said: "No. I think the key to the trade deficit is our competitiveness ... and very much world economic conditions."

"It's not a zero sum game," he added. "This is why we have such enormous stake in economic health in Europe, Japan, Asia (and) Latin America because if those areas are healthy, they buy more and it increases our exports and as they are slow, as Europe is slow right now and Japan is uncertain, that adversely affects our exports and increases our trade deficit."
Rubin said it was in the interests of both the United States and Japan that Japanese growth be strong.
"Clearly there's a concern that (Japanese) growth may slow down," he said.

"It is obviously overwhelmingly in the interest of Japan, but it's also very much in our interest, that Japan continue to have good growth and we believe it's very important that it be led by domestic demand."

"I think that given what's happening in Japan with respect to their fiscal situation, with the consumption tax, that it is very important to Japan, and also to us, that they be very watchful with respect to what's happening and take appropriate measures if need be," he added.
Rubin said he believed Clinton's budget for fiscal year 1998 was "good, strong, sound and sensible" and he believed it was likely there would be a balanced budget agreement.

"It's important for us to put out a serious budget and there's no question at least in my judgement that' we've done that and I presume it will be taken seriously by those who receive it," Rubin said.

"I'd say this budget has many similarities to the budget last year, but there are also differences," he added. "One of them obviously is the baseline, which makes a very big difference, but there are other differences as well."

Rubin declined to offer details on such differences, but said he believed it was likely the White House and Congress could reach a balanced budget deal, saying that the improved economic outlook was a key reason for this.

"I think not only should we reach a balanced budget, but it seems to me that we certainly should be able to do it this year," he added. Asked if this was likely, Rubin replied. "Yes, I do think it's likely -- now, likely is not certain."
